We'll connect player input to the physics engine, using C# scripts that read axes and button presses and then translate them into Rigidbody2D motion. OverlapCircle. I will also point out common mistakes that create jerky motion, like mixing transform. position with physics, or polling input only in FixedUpdate. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Player Movement & Input
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Player Movement & Input in 2D

Connect input polling to Rigidbody2D movement, use fixed-timestep physics, and integrate simple animations for clear player feedback.

In this lesson
Horizontal movement and jumping using Rigidbody2D.
Coming up
Ground checks with OverlapCircle and Animator links.
Practice
Hands-on activity: implement the PlayerController2D script.
Concept map
Input → State → Physics → Animation
Starter script preview
void Update()
{
  if (Input.GetButtonDown("Jump") && isGrounded)
  {
    rb.velocity = new Vector2(rb.velocity.x, jumpForce);
  }
}

void FixedUpdate()
{
  isGrounded = Physics2D.OverlapCircle(groundCheck.position, 0.2f, groundLayer);
  float moveInput = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
  rb.velocity = new Vector2(moveInput * moveSpeed, rb.velocity.y);
}
Why this matters

Predictable physics and responsive input are the foundation of platformer feel. Small timing or grounding errors break player trust.

Create a GroundCheck child, assign it near the player's feet, and set the groundLayer mask to include only your ground objects. This prevents missed ground detections and accidental triggers from non-ground colliders.

screens.title: Input and Movement Fundamentals
screens.narratorSegment: Movement begins with input values and ends with motion applied to a physics body. In Unity, Input. GetAxis("Horizontal") yields a continuous value from -1 to 1 that represents left and right input from keyboard, joystick, or controller. This axis value is the simplest abstraction for direction and magnitude; multiplying it by a moveSpeed gives a target horizontal velocity. Using Rigidbody2D. velocity to set the x component is a straightforward method: you preserve the current vertical velocity, and overwrite the horizontal component each physics step. A concrete example: when the axis returns 0.8 and moveSpeed is 5, the desired horizontal velocity becomes 4. That value is assigned to rb. velocity. x, and the physics solver handles collisions and gravity. A common misconception is that directly setting velocity removes physics; in fact, velocity acts as a controlled request to the physics solver and still respects collisions and gravity on the vertical axis. Key takeaway: use axis values for direction, scale by moveSpeed, and apply within the physics timestep for predictable results. Input and Movement Fundamentals means input.getaxis produces a continuous control value that you scale by movespeed and apply to rigidbody2d.velocity for smooth horizontal motion.. In practical terms, how input values turn into motion in a 2d platformer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Input & Movement
Definition

Axis → Velocity

Use Input.GetAxis("Horizontal") to read direction and scale that value by moveSpeed, then set the Rigidbody2D velocity on the physics tick.

Key points
  • Axis returns -1..1 for left/right input sources.
  • Multiply by moveSpeed to compute horizontal velocity.
  • Apply in FixedUpdate to keep physics consistent.
Example
If axis=0.8 and moveSpeed=5, set velocity.x to 4 so the body moves right with that linear speed.
Readable Code Snippet
void FixedUpdate()
{
  float moveInput = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
  rb.velocity = new Vector2(moveInput * moveSpeed, rb.velocity.y);
}
Misconception
Setting transform.position appears simple, but it bypasses the physics solver and can cause clipping or tunneling when collisions occur.
Takeaway
Use axis→velocity in FixedUpdate and preserve rb.velocity.y so gravity and jumps remain intact.

screens.title: FixedUpdate vs Update
screens.narratorSegment: A common source of bugs is treating Update and FixedUpdate as interchangeable. Update runs once per rendered frame and varies with frame rate. FixedUpdate runs at a fixed timestep synchronized with the physics solver. For stable physics-driven motion, sample input in Update for responsiveness, but apply forces or set Rigidbody2D properties in FixedUpdate. One practical workflow is: sample Input. GetAxis and Input. GetButtonDown in Update and store them in private variables; then, in FixedUpdate, use the stored axis value to compute velocity and apply jumps using a queued flag that was set on the frame the button was pressed. For jumping specifically, Input. GetButtonDown is frame-specific; if you sample it in Update and set a boolean like jumpRequested, you can consume that request in FixedUpdate and then clear it. This approach keeps input responsive to the player's quick taps while ensuring physics code runs at a consistent rate. Misusing these callbacks leads to missed inputs or inconsistent forces depending on frame timing. FixedUpdate vs Update means sample input in update, store results, and perform physics updates in fixedupdate so you keep responsiveness and deterministic physics behavior.. In practical terms, when to poll input and when to apply physics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Update vs FixedUpdate
Process

Input → Queue → Physics

Follow a two-step pattern: sample in Update, apply in FixedUpdate. This keeps short press inputs reliable and physics deterministic.
Step 1: Update
Read axis and one-shot buttons. Set flags like jumpRequested when a one-shot occurs.
Step 2: FixedUpdate
Consume stored input flags, set rb.velocity or AddForce, and clear jump flags. Physics executes reliably here.
Pattern Example
private float moveInput;
private bool jumpRequested;

void Update()
{
  moveInput = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
  if (Input.GetButtonDown("Jump")) jumpRequested = true;
}

void FixedUpdate()
{
  rb.velocity = new Vector2(moveInput * moveSpeed, rb.velocity.y);
  if (jumpRequested && isGrounded)
  {
    rb.velocity = new Vector2(rb.velocity.x, jumpForce);
    jumpRequested = false;
  }
}
Gotcha
If you read GetButtonDown only in FixedUpdate you may miss quick taps between physics steps; sample in Update instead.

keyIdea.text: Cache Rigidbody2D, poll Input.GetAxis, compute velocity.x = axis * moveSpeed, and apply inside FixedUpdate while preserving vertical velocity.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Horizontal Movement
Full snippet
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerMovement : MonoBehaviour
{
  public float moveSpeed = 5f;
  private Rigidbody2D rb;

  void Start()
  {
    rb = GetComponent();
  }

  void FixedUpdate()
  {
    float moveInput = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
    rb.velocity = new Vector2(moveInput * moveSpeed, rb.velocity.y);
  }
}
Explanation & Tips
  • GetComponent in Start caches the Rigidbody2D to avoid repeated calls.
  • Keep vertical velocity unchanged so gravity and jumps still apply.
  • Make moveSpeed public for quick tuning in the Inspector.
Pro tip
Clamp or smooth input if you need acceleration, but raw velocity assignment gives precise platformer control.

screens.title: Jumping and Ground Checks
screens.narratorSegment: Jumping requires gating the vertical impulse so the player can't jump endlessly. The typical pattern uses a small child Transform positioned at the character's feet, a groundLayer LayerMask, and Physics2D. OverlapCircle to check for any collider in that area. OverlapCircle returns non-null when it finds a collider on the specified layers, so you convert that to a boolean isGrounded. Use Input. GetButtonDown("Jump") in Update to detect the button press and then execute the jump in FixedUpdate if isGrounded is true. Apply the jump by setting rb. velocity = new Vector2(rb. velocity. x, jumpForce) for a precise immediate vertical velocity, or optionally use AddForce if you prefer impulse-based physics. A common mistake is using too large a radius for the overlap, which can detect walls as ground. Keep the radius small and verify placement visually. Final takeaway: a well-positioned ground check and a one-shot input lock produce tight, predictable jumps. Jumping and Ground Checks means use a groundcheck transform and physics2d.overlapcircle to gate input.getbuttondown so jumps happen only when isgrounded is true, then set rb.velocity.y to jumpforce.. In practical terms, use overlapcircle and isgrounded to control jump logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Jumping & Ground Checks
Ground check code
public Transform groundCheck;
public LayerMask groundLayer;
private bool isGrounded;

void FixedUpdate()
{
  isGrounded = Physics2D.OverlapCircle(groundCheck.position, 0.2f, groundLayer);
}

void Update()
{
  if (Input.GetButtonDown("Jump") && isGrounded)
  {
    rb.velocity = new Vector2(rb.velocity.x, jumpForce);
  }
}
Practical notes
  • Position groundCheck at the feet; a Y offset like -0.5 often works.
  • Use a small radius (e.g., 0.2) to avoid detecting walls or nearby objects.
  • Set groundLayer in the Inspector to include only ground colliders.
Common mistake
Forgetting to assign groundLayer causes isGrounded to always be false, so the player can never jump.

screens.title: Creating the GroundCheck GameObject
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable ground check starts in the Scene. Create an empty child GameObject under your Player and name it GroundCheck. Position it just below the player's feet — a relative Y offset around -0.4 to -0.6 is common, but exact values depend on collider size. In the PlayerController2D script, expose a public Transform groundCheck and drag this child object into that slot in the Inspector. Next, add a Layer named Ground and assign it to your floor tiles or terrain. Then set the groundLayer LayerMask in the script to include only this Ground layer. Run the scene and toggle the IsGrounded boolean in the Inspector (if public) to visually verify the OverlapCircle. If you still see misses, check that the radius is not too small and that colliders are not set to triggers unless intentionally used. This scene-setup process is often the difference between a working jump and a player that falls through the world. Step-by-step
  1. Create empty child named GroundCheck under Player.
  2. Position it around the player feet, e.g., Y = -0.5 relative.

screens.title: velocity vs AddForce
screens.narratorSegment: Two common ways to cause motion on a Rigidbody2D are directly setting velocity and applying forces. Setting rb. velocity gives immediate, deterministic control over linear speed and is ideal when you want precise platformer behavior: jumps that begin with a predictable vertical velocity or horizontal speeds that match tuning parameters exactly. AddForce, by contrast, applies an impulse or continuous force that the physics solver integrates over time. Use AddForce for emergent, physicsy interactions like being pushed by explosions or when you want momentum to accumulate naturally. A concrete example: for a crisp single-frame jump, set rb. velocity. y to jumpForce. For a physics-driven shove, call rb. AddForce(Vector2. up * force, ForceMode2D. Impulse). A misconception is that AddForce is always more realistic; while true for complex simulation, it can make simple platforming feel floaty and harder to tune. Choose the method that matches the desired control and feel. velocity vs AddForce means use velocity for precise, immediate control; use addforce for impulse-based or emergent physics interactions where momentum accumulation is desired.. In practical terms, when to set rigidbody2d.velocity and when to use addforce. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Flipping the Sprite
screens.narratorSegment: A simple and effective way to make a 2D sprite face left or right is to flip its horizontal scale. If your default sprite faces right, set transform. localScale. x to positive when moving right and negative when moving left. This approach mirrors the entire GameObject, so colliders and child objects move with it. Use Mathf. Abs to ensure you don't accidentally double-flip by negating an already negative value. Put the flip logic in the same place you consume horizontal input in FixedUpdate so the visual direction matches motion. Remember a common pitfall: if you have asymmetric child objects or a separate weapon mount, flipping localScale will mirror everything; in those cases you might flip only the sprite renderer or adjust child transforms to compensate. Flipping with localScale is inexpensive and avoids extra animator state complexity when only direction changes. Flipping the Sprite means flip the x component of transform.localscale based on moveinput sign; use mathf.abs to avoid compounded flips.. screens.title: Debugging Movement Issues
screens.narratorSegment: Movement bugs often reveal themselves as jerky motion, missed inputs, infinite jumps, or teleporting behavior during collisions. A frequent cause of teleporting is mixing transform. position changes with Rigidbody2D operations. If some code sets transform. position while physics also adjusts velocity, the solver can respond unpredictably. Move all physics changes into Rigidbody2D methods. Missed inputs often happen when GetButtonDown is read in FixedUpdate and the tap occurs between physics steps; sample it in Update and queue the action for FixedUpdate. Perpetual falling or inability to jump usually comes from a misconfigured groundLayer or a misplaced GroundCheck Transform; double-check the layer masks and overlap radius. Finally, tumbling can result from an unconstrained Z rotation—use RigidbodyConstraints2D. FreezeRotation to keep the player upright. Use OnDrawGizmos to visualize your overlap circle and confirm behavior in the editor. Systematic checks of layer assignment, callback placement, and transform usage resolve most problems quickly. screens.narratorSegment: Physical stability matters for player control. In 2D platformers it's common to freeze Z rotation on the Rigidbody2D so collisions do not cause the player to spin or tumble. content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Hands-on Activity
Starter script (replace content)
using UnityEngine;

public class PlayerController2D : MonoBehaviour
{
    public float moveSpeed = 5f;
    public float jumpForce = 10f;
    private Rigidbody2D rb;
    private bool isGrounded;

    public Transform groundCheck;
    public LayerMask groundLayer;

    void Start()
    {
        rb = GetComponent();
        if (groundCheck == null)
        {
            Debug.LogError("GroundCheck Transform not assigned!");
        }
    }

    void Update()
    {
        if (Input.GetButtonDown("Jump") && isGrounded)
        {
            rb.velocity = new Vector2(rb.velocity.x, jumpForce);
        }
    }

    void FixedUpdate()
    {
        isGrounded = Physics2D.OverlapCircle(groundCheck.position, 0.2f, groundLayer);
        float moveInput = Input.GetAxis("Horizontal");
        rb.velocity = new Vector2(moveInput * moveSpeed, rb.velocity.y);
    }
}
Scene checklist
  • Create Ground layer and assign to ground objects.
  • Add GroundCheck child and drag it into the script slot.
  • Set moveSpeed and jumpForce in Inspector for feel testing.
  • Freeze Z rotation on Rigidbody2D to prevent tumble.
Try this
Run the scene and press left/right and jump to confirm consistent behavior. Tweak values until controls feel responsive.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn the practical building blocks for responsive 2D player control. We'll connect player input to the physics engine, using C# scripts that read axes and button presses and then translate them into Rigidbody2D motion. You will see why physics code belongs in FixedUpdate while input polling stays in Update, how to prevent infinite jumping using a grounded check, and how to blend movement state with the Animator for visual feedback. A concrete example runs through horizontal movement with Input. GetAxis, jumping with Input. GetButtonDown limited by isGrounded, and a recommended ground-check technique using Physics2D. OverlapCircle. I will also point out common mistakes that create jerky motion, like mixing transform. position with physics, or polling input only in FixedUpdate. By the end, you should understand both a robust starter script and why each design choice matters for consistency and feel. Think about one small change you could make to improve control responsiveness in your next prototype.

By the end of this chapter you will implement a simple, reliable 2D player controller and understand the reasons behind each design choice. First, you will write input handling that captures horizontal axis values and one-shot jump presses so controls remain responsive. Second, you will apply physics operations inside FixedUpdate to keep motion stable across frame-rate differences. Third, you will construct a grounded check using a small child object and Physics2D. OverlapCircle to prevent infinite jumps and to trigger jump animation states. Finally, you will connect movement state to the Animator by setting speed and grounded parameters so the character visually reflects physics state. Each objective pairs a practical coding step with why it matters for player experience. As you work, verify competency by running the scene, adjusting moveSpeed and jumpForce in the Inspector, and observing how consistent the motion feels across runs. Think about what you would test first to confirm that your grounded check is correct.

This second objectives slide focuses on practice and common pitfalls. You will practice creating a GroundCheck child object and assigning a LayerMask so Physics2D. OverlapCircle reliably detects ground colliders. You will tune moveSpeed and jumpForce in the Inspector to feel right for your game, and you will learn to freeze z-rotation on the Rigidbody2D to prevent tumbling in collisions. You will also learn to separate input polling from physics updates: sample axes in Update, store them, and consume them in FixedUpdate. Finally, we emphasize testing: check the OverlapCircle radius and the ground layer assignment since a misplaced layer or wrong radius is a frequent cause of perpetual false negatives for isGrounded. These tasks train both coding and scene setup habits essential for stable platformer feel. Learning Objectives (Practice & Pitfalls) means create and position groundcheck, configure layermask, freeze unwanted rotation, and separate input polling from physics updates to avoid common movement bugs.. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Movement begins with input values and ends with motion applied to a physics body. In Unity, Input. GetAxis("Horizontal") yields a continuous value from -1 to 1 that represents left and right input from keyboard, joystick, or controller. This axis value is the simplest abstraction for direction and magnitude; multiplying it by a moveSpeed gives a target horizontal velocity. Using Rigidbody2D. velocity to set the x component is a straightforward method: you preserve the current vertical velocity, and overwrite the horizontal component each physics step. A concrete example: when the axis returns 0.8 and moveSpeed is 5, the desired horizontal velocity becomes 4. That value is assigned to rb. velocity. x, and the physics solver handles collisions and gravity. A common misconception is that directly setting velocity removes physics; in fact, velocity acts as a controlled request to the physics solver and still respects collisions and gravity on the vertical axis. Key takeaway: use axis values for direction, scale by moveSpeed, and apply within the physics timestep for predictable results. Input and Movement Fundamentals means input.getaxis produces a continuous control value that you scale by movespeed and apply to rigidbody2d.velocity for smooth horizontal motion.. In practical terms, how input values turn into motion in a 2d platformer. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A common source of bugs is treating Update and FixedUpdate as interchangeable. Update runs once per rendered frame and varies with frame rate. FixedUpdate runs at a fixed timestep synchronized with the physics solver. For stable physics-driven motion, sample input in Update for responsiveness, but apply forces or set Rigidbody2D properties in FixedUpdate. One practical workflow is: sample Input. GetAxis and Input. GetButtonDown in Update and store them in private variables; then, in FixedUpdate, use the stored axis value to compute velocity and apply jumps using a queued flag that was set on the frame the button was pressed. For jumping specifically, Input. GetButtonDown is frame-specific; if you sample it in Update and set a boolean like jumpRequested, you can consume that request in FixedUpdate and then clear it. This approach keeps input responsive to the player's quick taps while ensuring physics code runs at a consistent rate. Misusing these callbacks leads to missed inputs or inconsistent forces depending on frame timing. FixedUpdate vs Update means sample input in update, store results, and perform physics updates in fixedupdate so you keep responsiveness and deterministic physics behavior.. In practical terms, when to poll input and when to apply physics. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Two common ways to cause motion on a Rigidbody2D are directly setting velocity and applying forces. Setting rb. velocity gives immediate, deterministic control over linear speed and is ideal when you want precise platformer behavior: jumps that begin with a predictable vertical velocity or horizontal speeds that match tuning parameters exactly. AddForce, by contrast, applies an impulse or continuous force that the physics solver integrates over time. Use AddForce for emergent, physicsy interactions like being pushed by explosions or when you want momentum to accumulate naturally. A concrete example: for a crisp single-frame jump, set rb. velocity. y to jumpForce. For a physics-driven shove, call rb. AddForce(Vector2. up * force, ForceMode2D. Impulse). Movement bugs often reveal themselves as jerky motion, missed inputs, infinite jumps, or teleporting behavior during collisions. A frequent cause of teleporting is mixing transform. position changes with Rigidbody2D operations. If some code sets transform. position while physics also adjusts velocity, the solver can respond unpredictably. Move all physics changes into Rigidbody2D methods. Missed inputs often happen when GetButtonDown is read in FixedUpdate and the tap occurs between physics steps; sample it in Update and queue the action for FixedUpdate.
